paper_sections.title: Similar neural mechanisms for perceptual guesses and free decisions

description.value: The study investigated whether perceptual guesses and unconstrained free decisions share neural representations by using fMRI searchlight pattern classification and cross-condition prediction.

design.value: An event-related fMRI study in which participants made category choices about pianos and chairs using three different conditions: high-visibility perceptual choices, zero-visibility perceptual guesses, and free choices.

description.value: Questionnaires assessed adherence to the task instructions and success of the experimental manipulation, including whether participants noticed the missing object images and whether they confused the free-decision and perceptual conditions.
Interviews assessed awareness of the missing object images and the timing of free decisions and perceptual guesses.

source_definition.value: The three experimental conditions were the high visibility condition, the perceptual guessing condition, and the free decision condition.

task_name.value: category choices about pianos and chairs

task_description.value: Participants completed an event-related fMRI experiment with high-visibility perceptual choices, perceptual guesses under zero visibility, and free choices. Each trial consisted of a brief standing wave of the same mask–target–mask sequence repeated three times, with a white fixation cross centrally superimposed. Participants made six runs of 72 trials, with an equal number of trials per condition in each run.

instructions.value: For the high visibility and perceptual guessing conditions, participants categorized the object as a piano or chair. For the perceptual guessing condition, they were told that an object stimulus was presented, albeit that it was sometimes difficult to detect. For the free decision condition, participants were instructed to spontaneously choose the category that first came to their mind, independent of the presentation; they were told to choose an object category instead of a response button, not change their mind after making a decision, and always make a decision even if uncertain.

stimuli.value: The stimuli were 24 pictures of pianos and chairs, transformed into grey-scale versions with a size of 400 × 400 pixels. Two different scrambled masks were used during presentation. The perceptual guessing and free decision conditions used one strongly masked noise image consisting of scrambled phase textures; all noise trials used the same noise stimulus.

task_performance_measures.value: hit rate for visible pianos and chairs

instrument.value: Siemens TRIO 3 T scanner (Erlangen, Germany) with a standard head coil

description.value: Functional MRI volumes of the whole brain were acquired. Each run acquired 208 volumes; six runs were performed for each participant. The first two volumes of every scan were discarded by default to allow for magnetic saturation effects.

Motion-corrected and unsmoothed brain images were used for the GLM and subsequent searchlight decoding. The resulting decoding maps were normalized to a standard stereotaxic space using the Montreal Neurological Institute EPI template and smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 6 mm FWHM.

description.value: For the univariate analyses, all data were motion corrected to the first volume of the first run, normalized to MNI space, resampled to 3 × 3 × 3 mm voxels, and smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 8 mm FWHM.

model_settings.value: For each run, trials were modelled as events beginning with the presentation of the cue. Trials were assigned to piano and chair trials according to participants' choices in all three conditions in separate analyses. The model captured both the cue and object periods.

model_type.value: multivariate pattern classification using a linear support vector pattern classifier

model_settings.value: For each central voxel, a searchlight cluster was defined as a sphere with radius 4 voxels. GLM parameter estimates were extracted for the searchlight voxels for each category and run. The classifier used a fixed regularisation parameter C = 1 and was trained on all runs but one and tested on the remaining independent run. Six-fold cross-validation was performed. The same number of exemplars for each decision and run was used for decoding.

estimator.value: six-fold cross-validation with an independent left-out run as the test data set

model_settings.value: Mean probability of correct classification was combined into three-dimensional maps of local decoding accuracy for each condition and participant. Random-effects group-level analyses were computed on a voxel-by-voxel basis to identify searchlight positions where local patterns had significant decoding accuracy across all participants.

Pattern vectors from one condition were used to train the classifier to distinguish piano and chair choices and to predict decisions in the left-out run from the other condition. Both directions of cross-condition classification were performed for the perceptual guessing and free decision conditions, followed by an ANOVA and an inclusive conjunction test.

Modelling was the same as for the multivariate analyses, resulting in separate regressors for piano and chair trials, individually for each experimental condition and each run. Contrasts between pianos and chairs were calculated for each condition, and the three experimental conditions were contrasted across object categories.

Two-tailed t-tests for independent samples tested whether the BI high and BI low groups differed in average whole-brain searchlight decoding accuracy and in decoding accuracy for the best searchlight clusters.

description.value: On each trial the sequence contained an object image, either a piano or chair, that was clearly visible. Participants were asked to identify the category of the presented object. The object was preceded by a 150 ms pre-mask, presented for 66.7 ms, and followed by a 433.3 ms post-mask.

Participants were given the same categorization task but the timing of the stimuli was chosen to yield strong masking. The sequence contained only a neutral noise image instead of an object, although participants were told that an object stimulus was presented and believed they were making difficult perceptual guesses. The noise image was preceded by a 150 ms pre-mask, presented for 16.7 ms, and followed by a 483.3 ms post-mask.

The presentation was identical to the low visibility condition and contained the same strongly masked noise image. Participants were asked to spontaneously and freely choose either piano or chair, whatever category came first to their minds, while ignoring the visual stimulus display.
